# Supplementary Note S1. Data, D2 target construction, quality control and sampling

VIIRS active-fire detections from Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 are acquired as 375-m cross-track swaths from NASA FIRMS [@nasa_firms]. At the swath edge the projected pixel can reach approximately 1.6 km along scan and 0.8 km along track, producing the geometric Bow-Tie effect: repeated detections of the same fire, dilution of fire radiative power (FRP) over a larger apparent area and incorrect assignment to the national 1-km² grid [@schroeder2014]. The implemented kinematic filter is

$$\mathcal{D}_{\text{filtered}} = \left\{ f \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{raw}} \mid \text{scan}(f) \le 1.5\ \text{km} \;\land\; \text{confidence}(f) \neq \text{'low'} \right\}.$$

The observed maximum scan in the study window was 0.8 km, so the rule removed no records but remains active for orbital windows with larger view angles. Duplicate overpasses on the same civil date are consolidated by 1-km² cell, retaining `num_focos_dia`, `max_frp_dia` and `sum_frp_dia`.

D2 separates primary ignition from tactical propagation. Let $F_t$ be the set of cells with a thermal detection on day $t$. D2 ignition at cell $i$ and day $t$ requires (i) $i \in F_t$, (ii) no cell in $F_{t-1}$ within 25 km and (iii) no detection in cell $i$ during the preceding 10 days. D2 propagation requires $i \in F_t$ and at least one cell in $F_{t-1}$ within 25 km. Same-cell detections recurring within 2–10 days without an active neighbor within 25 km on day $t-1$—typically multi-day smoldering holdovers or cloud-obscured satellite omissions—are not assigned to either positive target set; they remain candidate negatives, which prevents holdover persistence from entering the ignition target. The two target sets are disjoint. The 25-km threshold defines the target domain and is not a negative-sampling buffer; no 20-km buffer is applied to the test set. The 20-km buffer is used only in the spatial block holdout.

The case-control sample is drawn at 1:10 per task and region. Training uses 2018–2022, validation uses 2023 and the test is the frozen 2024–2025 period. Population denominators are kept separately and are used for prior correction. The same test rows are used for every model, FWI and INPE, so comparisons are paired. Sampling counts and class ratios are in Table S10. The variable dictionary is in Table S1; the full audit log is in Table S15.

Data quality checks collapse duplicate VIIRS overpasses, remove `low`-confidence detections, reconstruct daily precipitation from sub-daily increments and reject impossible values above 300 mm/day. ERA5-Land nodes [@munoz2021era5land] are mapped to cells with a precomputed cKDTree. The processed data archive contains test targets, probabilities, benchmark layers, sampling plans and trained artifacts, so the result tables can be regenerated without the raw multi-terabyte archive.

# Supplementary Note S2. Bounded monotonic Platt calibration and hyperparameters

Let $z_i \in \mathbb{R}$ be the margin produced by the LightGBM ensemble [@ke2017lightgbm] for cell $i$, and let $y_i \in \{0,1\}$ be the binary fire label. Standard Platt scaling [@platt1999] estimates $w,b \in \mathbb{R}$ by minimizing binary cross-entropy:

$$\mathcal{L}(w,b) = -\sum_{i=1}^{M} \left[ y_i \log \sigma(w z_i + b) + (1-y_i)\log(1-\sigma(w z_i + b)) \right], \qquad \sigma(v)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-v}}.$$

If and only if $w>0$, the map $p(z)=\sigma(w z+b)$ is strictly increasing and preserves the ranking of the ensemble. Its derivative is

$$\frac{dp}{dz}=w\,\sigma(w z+b)\,[1-\sigma(w z+b)],$$

and the sigmoid factor is strictly positive, so $\operatorname{sign}(dp/dz)=\operatorname{sign}(w)$. A positive slope therefore leaves ROC-AUC unchanged. Unconstrained logistic regression can converge to $w<0$ under extreme imbalance or bimodal margins, inverting the ranking and turning a ROC-AUC of 0.77 into 0.23.

The implementation minimizes a bounded Brier loss with L-BFGS-B in `src/modelo.py`:

$$\min_{w,b}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\left(y_i-\frac{1}{1+\exp(-(w z_i+b))}\right)^2,\qquad 0.10\le w\le 10.00,\quad -10.0\le b\le 10.0.$$

The lower bound guarantees strict monotonicity and prevents gradient collapse in asymptotic regions. Calibration is fitted on 2023 and frozen for 2024–2025. The same cutoff logic is used for M1, M2, M3 and propagation; cutoffs are selected on validation with an F0.5 criterion and applied after prior correction. Hyperparameters are in Table S2. The ablation uses a common capacity (45/60 rounds and 23/31 leaves) to isolate the feature effect.

# Supplementary Note S3. Evaluation protocol and extended analyses

The harness is fixed before the test is opened. It contains five components:

**(1)** A strictly temporal split: training 2018–2022, validation 2023 and test 2024–2025.

**(2)** A 50-km spatial block holdout with a 20-km buffer; priors are recomputed without held-out fires.

**(3)** A paired bootstrap grouped by date ($B=1\,000$) for confidence intervals and differences against FWI [@vanwagner1987] and INPE [@setzer2019].

**(4)** A lead-time analysis using t-1 weather to quantify the nowcast-to-forecast gap.

**(5)** Population-level, conformal and cost-loss analyses.

Bootstrap resampling is by date, not by row, because daily fire activity is strongly clustered. All cells from a sampled date are retained; this preserves within-day dependence. The spatial holdout removes an entire 50-km block plus a 20-km buffer, recomputes historical priors without the held-out fires and evaluates both held-in and held-out cells. The primary metrics are ROC-AUC and PR-AUC; Brier score, expected calibration error, precision, recall, F0.5 and false positives are also reported. AUC intervals use 500 grouped bootstrap replicates; paired differences use 1 000. The six confirmatory comparisons are corrected with Holm–Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg; all remain significant at α = 0.05. The bootstrap resolution is 0.001, so adjusted values at the floor are upper bounds.

The full benchmark is in Table S11 and its continuation, paired significance in Table S7, the complete spatial block results in Table S8 and the lead-time results in Table S9. Seed/capacity stability, the rolling-origin backtest and adversarial validation are in Tables S25, S26 and S29 and Figure S5; threshold sensitivity is in Table S14 (continuation) and Figure S6. The controlled ablation is in Table S12 and Figure S2; SHAP is in Table S13 and Figure S1; population evaluation is in Table S6; conformal coverage is in Table S5; cost-loss is in Table S14 and Figure S3. The computational profile is in Table S4. All analyses use the frozen test rows archived with the code release.

# Supplementary Note S4. Implementation of the FWI and INPE indices

This note documents the two benchmark indices exactly as they are implemented. The full Canadian FWI is produced by `scripts/02d_calcular_fwi_completo.py` from `src/fwi.py`; the INPE Risco de Fogo by `scripts/02e_calcular_inpe.py` from `src/inpe.py`; the benchmark joins both to the 1-km grid by `nodo_clima_id` and `fecha` in `scripts/13_benchmarking_modelos.py`. Neither index was fitted to the fire labels.

## S4.1 Canadian Fire Weather Index

### Fuel codes

The standard six-code system is implemented without a custom fuel type:

- **FFMC (Fine Fuel Moisture Code):** moisture of surface litter and fine fuels (approximately the top 1–2 cm); scale 0–101.
- **DMC (Duff Moisture Code):** moisture of the loosely compacted organic layer; medium-term drying.
- **DC (Drought Code):** moisture of the deep, compacted organic layer; seasonal drought storage.
- **BUI (Buildup Index):** fuel available for combustion, derived from DMC and DC.
- **ISI (Initial Spread Index):** initial spread potential, derived from FFMC and wind.
- **FWI (Fire Weather Index):** frontal fire intensity, derived from ISI and BUI.

### Equations

Let $F_t$, $D_t$ and $Q_t$ be FFMC, DMC and DC on day $t$; let $T$ be the 15:00 UTC temperature (°C), $H$ the corresponding relative humidity (%), $W$ the 10-m wind speed (km h⁻¹) and $r$ the 00–24 h rainfall (mm). The recursion is applied per node in chronological order.

The fine-fuel moisture content is

$$m_{t-1}=\frac{147.2(101-F_{t-1})}{59.5+F_{t-1}}.$$

For $r>0.5$ mm, with $r_f=r-0.5$,

$$m_0=m_{t-1}+42.5\,r_f\,e^{-100/(251-m_{t-1})}\left(1-e^{-6.93/r_f}\right)+\epsilon,$$

where $\epsilon=0.0015(m_{t-1}-150)^2\sqrt{r_f}$ is the small correction term coded in `src/fwi.py`; $m_0$ is capped at 250. The equilibrium moisture contents are

$$E_d=0.942H^{0.679}+11e^{(H-100)/10}+0.18(21.1-T)(1-e^{-0.115H}),$$

$$E_w=0.614H^{0.753}+10e^{(H-100)/10}+0.18(21.1-T)(1-e^{-0.115H}).$$

The drying and wetting rates are

$$k_d=\left[0.424\left(1-\left(\frac{100-H}{100}\right)^{1.7}\right)+0.0694\sqrt{W}\left(1-\left(\frac{100-H}{100}\right)^8\right)\right]0.581e^{0.0365T},$$

$$k_w=\left[0.424\left(1-\left(\frac{H}{100}\right)^{1.7}\right)+0.0694\sqrt{W}\left(1-\left(\frac{H}{100}\right)^8\right)\right]0.581e^{0.0365T}.$$

The moisture content after one day is

$$m_t=\begin{cases}E_d+(m_0-E_d)10^{-k_d}, & m_0<E_d,\\E_w+(m_0-E_w)10^{-k_w}, & m_0>E_w,\\m_0, & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$

and

$$F_t=\operatorname{clip}\left(\frac{59.5(250-m_t)}{147.2+m_t},\,0,\,101\right).$$

For DMC, when $r>1.5$ mm,

$$r_e=0.92r-1.27,\qquad m_0=20+280e^{-0.023D_{t-1}},$$

$$b=\begin{cases}100/(0.5+0.3D_{t-1}), & D_{t-1}\le33,\\14-1.3\ln D_{t-1}, & 33<D_{t-1}\le65,\\6.2\ln D_{t-1}-17.2, & D_{t-1}>65,\end{cases}$$

$$m_r=m_0+\frac{1000r_e}{48.77+br_e},\qquad D'=43.43(5.6348-\ln(m_r-20)),$$

with $D'$ floored at zero; when $r\le1.5$ mm, $D'=D_{t-1}$. The daily update uses

$$T_+=\max(T,-1.1),\qquad H_c=\operatorname{clip}(H,1,100),$$

$$K=1.894(T_++1.1)(100-H_c)L_e10^{-4},\qquad D_t=D'+K,$$

where $L_e$ is the effective day-length factor. For the study domain (20°S), the twelve monthly values are $L_e=(10.1,9.6,9.1,8.5,8.1,7.8,7.9,8.3,8.9,9.4,9.9,10.2)$.

For DC, when $r>2.8$ mm,

$$r_d=0.83r-1.27,\qquad Q_0=800e^{-Q_{t-1}/400}+3.937r_d,$$

with $Q_0$ capped at 800 and $Q'=400\ln(800/Q_0)$; otherwise $Q'=Q_{t-1}$. Then

$$Q_t=Q'+\frac{0.36\max(T,-2.8)+L_f}{2},$$

where $L_f$ is the day-length factor for DC. For 20°S, $L_f=(6.4,5.0,2.4,0.4,-1.6,-1.6,-1.6,-1.6,-1.6,0.9,3.8,5.8)$; the update is floored at zero.

BUI is

$$U_t=0 \quad \text{if } D_t\le0,$$

$$U_t=\frac{0.8D_tQ_t}{D_t+0.4Q_t} \quad \text{if } D_t\le0.4Q_t,$$

$$U_t=D_t-\left(1-\frac{0.8Q_t}{D_t+0.4Q_t}\right)\cdot\left(0.92+(0.0114D_t)^{1.7}\right) \quad \text{otherwise.}$$

ISI is

$$m=\frac{147.2(101-F_t)}{59.5+F_t},\qquad f_W=e^{0.05039W},$$

$$f_F=91.9e^{-0.1386m}\left(1+\frac{m^{5.31}}{4.93\times10^7}\right),\qquad R_t=0.208f_Wf_F.$$

Finally,

$$f_D=0.626U_t^{0.809}+2 \quad \text{if } U_t\le80,$$

$$f_D=\frac{1000}{25+108.64e^{-0.023U_t}} \quad \text{if } U_t>80,$$

$$B_t=0.1R_tf_D,$$

$$FWI_t=e^{2.72(0.434\ln B_t)^{0.647}} \quad \text{if } B_t>1,$$

$$FWI_t=B_t \quad \text{if } B_t\le1.$$

### Meteorology, timing and resolution

The 15:00 UTC fields (approximately local noon) are extracted from the ERA5-Land 3-hourly archive [@munoz2021era5land]: 2-m temperature, 2-m dew point, and the 10-m wind components $u_{10}$ and $v_{10}$. Relative humidity is derived from temperature and dew point with the Tetens saturation vapor pressure $e_s=0.61078e^{17.27T/(T+237.3)}$ and $H=100e_a/e_s$, clipped to 1–100 %. Wind speed is $W=3.6\sqrt{u_{10}^2+v_{10}^2}$ km h⁻¹. Rainfall is the 00–24 h total from the daily climate table.

The FWI uses **same-day** meteorology, not $t-1$: the codes for day $t$ are driven by the 15:00 UTC fields and the rainfall of day $t$. This is a nowcast configuration. The lagged $t-1$ experiment used to quantify the lead-time gap is a separate analysis (Note S3) and does not enter the benchmark.

The climate analysis uses a 0.25° node grid (640 nodes). Each node is matched to the nearest ERA5-Land pixel, and each 1-km² cell inherits one node through `nodo_clima_id`; the mapping is precomputed with a cKDTree. The full FWI series is stored in `fwi_completo_diario.parquet`. The `ffmc` and `isi` columns used as features by M1/M2/M3 are a separate daily approximation computed by `src/clima.py` from daily maximum temperature, VPD-derived relative humidity, daily maximum wind and daily rainfall; they are not the same series as the benchmark FWI.

### Initialization and warm-up

At the first day of each node series (1 January 2018) the codes are initialized as $F=85$, $D=6$ and $Q=15$. The recursion is then run continuously through 2025. No pre-2018 spin-up is available and no separate warm-up window is discarded: the 2018 calendar year is used only in the training split, so any initialization transient is confined to training. By the 2023 validation and the 2024–2025 test the codes have been iterated for at least five years, and the memory of the initial values is negligible.

## S4.2 INPE Risco de Fogo (2019)

The implementation follows the INPE 2019 version 11 formulation [@setzer2019]. The public product applies a correction for hotspots in the previous three days; that correction is deliberately omitted here because it would leak the ignition label. The benchmark therefore uses the weather-only formulation.

### Dryness index (PSE)

Let $r_j$ be daily rainfall and let

$$R_k(t)=\sum_{j=t-k+1}^{t}r_j$$

be the rainfall accumulated over the $k$ days ending on day $t$, with days before 1 January 2018 treated as zero. The PSE (período de secura; 0–105) is

$$PSE_t=105\prod_{j=1}^{11}\exp\left[-\lambda_j\left(R_{k_j}(t)-R_{k_{j-1}}(t)\right)\right],$$

with $R_0=0$, windows $k=(1,2,3,4,5,10,15,30,60,90,120)$ and coefficients

$$\lambda=(0.14,0.07,0.04,0.03,0.02,0.01,0.008,0.004,0.002,0.001,0.0007).$$

The 120-day window is left-truncated at the start of the 2018 series and is complete after 120 days. PSE is driven by same-day rainfall, not $t-1$.

### Flammability constant and basic risk

The primary specification uses a local, land-cover-weighted constant

$$A=\frac{6.0f_p+3.0f_s+1.72f_{ds}+1.72f_{dh}+1.5f_{pa}}{f_p+f_s+f_{ds}+f_{dh}+f_{pa}},$$

where $f_p$, $f_s$, $f_{ds}$, $f_{dh}$ and $f_{pa}$ are the MapBiomas percentages of pasture, savanna, dry forest, humid forest and palm [@mapbiomas2023]. If the denominator is zero, $A=0$. The basic risk is

$$R_b=0.8\frac{1+\sin\left(\min\left(\frac{A\,PSE_t}{120},2\right)\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}{2}.$$

The local $A$ is the primary version; a fixed $A=3.0$ (the INPE open-savanna coefficient) is reported as a sensitivity in Table S22.

### Observed risk and timing

The observed risk is

$$RF_t=\operatorname{clip}\left(R_bF_{UR}F_TF_{lat}F_{alt},\,0,\,1\right),$$

with

$$F_{UR}=1.3-0.006H_{min},\qquad F_T=0.4+0.02T_{max},$$

$$F_{lat}=1+0.003|\phi|,\qquad F_{alt}=1+0.00003z,$$

where $H_{min}$ and $T_{max}$ are the same-day daily minimum relative humidity and maximum temperature, $\phi$ is latitude and $z$ is elevation (m). The 1-km grid table does not carry elevation, so $F_{alt}=1$ in the benchmark. The INPE series is stored in `inpe_diario.parquet`; it uses the same-day daily fields and the same 0.25° node-to-cell mapping as the FWI. No $t-1$ lag is applied.

## S4.3 Calibration and operating points

**No local calibration was applied to either index.** The FWI remains on the Canadian index scale and INPE on a 0–1 risk scale; neither is a calibrated probability. For ignition in each region, the operating cutoff was selected on 2023 validation by maximizing F0.5 and then frozen for 2024–2025 (Tables S11 and S22). The local $A$ weighting is a land-cover parameterization, not a calibration to fire observations.

# Supplementary Note S5. Robustness analyses

This note documents the protocols behind Tables S25–S32 and Figures S5–S7. All analyses use the frozen 2018–2025 data and the same feature definitions as the main models unless stated otherwise.

## S5.1 Rolling-origin backtest

Four folds were evaluated for test years $Y=2022,\dots,2025$. In each fold, models were trained through $Y-2$, calibrated and thresholded on $Y-1$, and evaluated on $Y$. M1, M2 and M3 were retrained with the operational capacity of Table S2; the F0.5 cutoff was selected on $Y-1$ and frozen for $Y$. ROC-AUC and PR-AUC were computed on the case-control test rows. The M3−M2 ROC-AUC difference uses a paired bootstrap grouped by date ($B=1\,000$). The fold construction is strictly nested, so no test year contributes to training or threshold selection (Table S26; Figure S5).

## S5.2 Seed and capacity stability

M2 and M3 were trained with seeds 42, 7, 13, 21 and 33 and two capacities: the operational configuration and a +20 % variant in `num_leaves` and `num_boost_round` (Chaco 28/54; Oriental 37/72). All other hyperparameters were fixed. ROC-AUC and PR-AUC were evaluated on the frozen test. ΔROC is M3−M2 within the same seed and capacity; the table reports the mean, standard deviation, range, a t interval for the mean and the fraction of positive runs (Table S25).

## S5.3 Threshold and metric sensitivity

For M3 ignition and the propagation model, cutoffs were selected on 2023 validation by maximizing F0.5, F1, F2 and Youden's J. Precision, recall, F0.5, F1 and F2 were then evaluated on the 2024–2025 test. Figure S6 shows the validation curves; Table S14 (continued) reports the test metrics. The operational F0.5 cutoff is retained for the main tables; this analysis tests whether the ranking depends on that choice.

## S5.4 Adversarial validation

A LightGBM classifier was trained to separate training rows (2018–2022) from test rows (2024–2025) using the M3 feature set. Five stratified folds were used, with 100 boosting rounds, 31 leaves, learning rate 0.05 and gain importance. The reported AUC is the mean across folds; the top features are ranked by mean gain. Adversarial AUC measures distribution shift and is not a performance metric for the fire model (Table S29).

## S5.5 Negative control and permutation importance

The negative control retrains M3 after randomly permuting the training labels while keeping the features and validation labels unchanged; each reported value uses one fixed permutation of the training rows (`seed = 123`), with validation labels unchanged. A correctly specified, leakage-free pipeline should yield an AUC near 0.5. The control was repeated with and without the historical features (`dist_foco_hist_km`, `densidad_hist_25km`, `freq_hist_1km`). Permutation importance shuffles each feature, or each feature family, on the test rows and records the mean drop in ROC-AUC over three repeats. Families are weather, fuel, anthropogenic, historical and calendar. The control and permutation results are in Table S32 and Figure S7. An AUC above 0.5 in the control indicates residual cell-level or feature information; it is a diagnostic of what the score can and cannot support, not a substitute for the main ranking.

## S5.6 Gate thresholds and the no-gate sample

The baseline gate is fuel and VPD ≥ 0.8 kPa with 48-h rainfall < 10 mm. Stricter variants use VPD ≥ 1.0/1.2 kPa and rainfall < 5/2 mm. A no-gate ignition sample was generated from the full candidate archive with the same D2 operator, a 1:10 ratio and no biophysical filter (Table S31). Positives are all D2 ignitions in the sampled domain; negatives are all non-fire candidates. The no-gate sample is independent of the frozen gated sample; validation and test years are unchanged. FWI is evaluated on the same retained rows.

## S5.7 Sampling-ratio sensitivity

The 1:5 sample was obtained by downsampling training negatives from the frozen 1:10 sample. The 1:20 sample was generated independently from the full candidate archive with the baseline gate and 20 negatives per positive. Validation and test remain at 1:10 so ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and the prevalence-corrected population precision are comparable across training ratios (Table S28). The 1:5 and 1:20 analyses change the training class balance only.

## S5.8 VIIRS label-quality variants

The raw FIRMS archive (2018–2025) was filtered to scan ≤ 1.5 km and non-low confidence; the FIRMS type field was retained and is not used as a D2 exclusion. Two variants were built: high confidence (`h`) and FRP ≥ 10 MW. The variants were applied to the positive rows of the frozen 1:10 sample; negatives were unchanged. This is a label sensitivity, not a full reconstruction of D2 under the variant fire masks: removing a low-confidence or low-FRP detection can also change the t−1 buffer and the recent-fire state. The cloud-cover < 40 % variant is not reported because FIRMS lacks a cloud mask and the ERA5 total-cloud proxy did not complete in the CDS queue (Table S30).

## S5.9 Clean-environment verification

A separate Python 3.12 environment was created from `requirements-lock.txt`. The 76-test suite passed, and `shasum -a 256 -c auditoria/HASHES.sha256` returned OK. The run is recorded in `auditoria/R12_VERIFICACION_ENTORNO_LIMPIO.md`. The hashes cover the generated tables, figures, manuscript sources and analysis scripts.

---

The 1-km² grid is the modeling unit. Fuel fractions come from annual MapBiomas Collection 2 maps (2017–2023), joined to each row with the prior-year map; 2024 uses 2023 with lag 1 and 2025 reuses 2023 with lag 2 [@mapbiomas2023]. Historical priors use a causal three-year rolling window rather than the full 2018–2022 record. `rafaga_max_kmh` is a linear proxy and is not used as a feature. M3 contains 44 variables in the Chaco and 45 in the Oriental Region; M2 contains 35 and M1 contains 24.

The full benchmark includes M2, propagation, FWI, INPE and the climatological baseline; its continuation adds a GBT with the M3 features plus both indices. FWI and INPE are normalized indices, not calibrated probabilities. The weather-only GBT uses the same learner, capacity and calibration as M1/M2/M3 but only the FWI information set; its full detail is in Table S21. All cutoffs, including those of FWI and INPE, were selected on the 2023 validation set by maximizing F0.5 and then frozen for the 2024–2025 test; neither index received local calibration. The INPE constant A is land-cover-weighted (local A); Table S22 repeats the benchmark with a fixed A = 3.0 and shows that the ranking conclusion is unchanged. FWI is reported on the Canadian index scale (3.1285 in Chaco, 20.4720 in Oriental) and INPE on a 0–1 risk scale (0.0364 in Chaco, 0.0596 in Oriental).

$\alpha=C/L$ is the ratio of false-alarm cost to avoided loss; $V(\alpha)$ is the normalized value. This is a simple decision model, not an estimate of agency budgets. TP, FP and FN are expressed as fractions of the population; rows with $V(\alpha)=0$ are retained for completeness. M2 = baseline ignition model in the ignition task and tactical propagation model in the propagation task; M3 = hybrid ignition model.

**Table S22.** Sensitivity of the INPE Fire Risk to the flammability constant A on the retrospective 2024–2025 test. The primary version uses the land-cover-weighted A from MapBiomas fractions (local A, cell-specific); the sensitivity version fixes A = 3.0, the INPE coefficient for open savanna, for every cell. Cutoffs were selected on 2023 validation by maximizing F0.5 and frozen for 2024–2025, so precision, recall and F0.5 refer to different operating points and are not directly comparable across rows. ΔROC is fixed A minus local A, with a paired date-grouped bootstrap (B = 1 000); positive values favor the fixed version. Both versions remain far below M3 (ROC-AUC 0.8021/0.7534; Table 2). In the test sample, local A averages 2.89 in Chaco and 3.71 in Oriental.

## S5.10 External spatial validation in Boquerón

The leave-one-department-out pilot excluded Boquerón and a 25-km buffer from training and validation. Causal historical priors were recomputed with `excluir_cell_ids` for the excluded cells. M2 and M3 were retrained with the operational capacity; calibration and the F0.5 cutoff used 2023 rows outside the excluded area. FWI and INPE cutoffs were selected on the same 2023 rows. Evaluation used the 2024–2025 Boquerón rows (66 845 sampled rows; 5 038 positives). Metrics are reported both case-control and population-weighted; the latter use department-level D2 counts reconstructed from the full candidate archive because `conteos_poblacionales_d2.parquet` stores denominators by region. The buffer sensitivity uses 20, 25 and 30 km (Table S33b). This is a spatial external validation within Paraguay, not a cross-country validation.

## S5.11 Cross-country validation in Formosa (G0)

G0-Formosa was designed as a pre-registered, conditional cross-country test of the frozen M2/M3-Chaco system. The domain contains 75 236 cells of 1 km² (75 229 km²). The case-control test has 68 959 rows and 6 269 positive D2 ignition cell-days (2024: 3 429; 2025: 2 840); the 1:10 sampling matches the Paraguay design. M2/M3 boosters were frozen for G0-Z, and G0-C recalibrated Platt scaling and the F0.5 cutoff on Formosa 2023 only. G0-R retrained both models on Paraguay plus Formosa 2018–2022 and evaluated 2024–2025.

The primary soil/land-cover harmonization (H-A) maps MapBiomas Argentina classes 3/4/6 to `pct_bosque_seco`, 9 to plantation, 11/73 to wetland, 10/12/63/66/77 to savanna, 15 to pasture, 18/19/36 to agriculture and 22/24/25/26/33/34 to non-combustible. Class 6 (flooded forest) is 22.3 % of the area and 42.9 % of VIIRS detections. H-B (class 6 → wetland) and H-C (mask cells with ≥50 % class 6) are sensitivities. The crosswalk is archived in `auditoria/G0/crosswalk_mapbiomas_argentina.csv`.

In 2024, M2/M3 reached ROC-AUC 0.7133/0.7245 and PR-AUC 0.1839/0.1943; the paired M3−M2 ΔROC was +0.0112 (95 % CI +0.0065–+0.0155). In 2025, M2/M3 reached 0.7050/0.7112 and 0.1735/0.1716, with ΔROC +0.0062 (95 % CI −0.0001–+0.0129). G0-C reduced ECE to 0.0078–0.0153, but the local cutoff lowered M3's F0.5 in 2025. Neither arm reached the pre-registered transport threshold of ROC-AUC > 0.75. G0-R improved M3 ROC-AUC only to 0.7275/0.7150 and did not remove the 2025 uncertainty. H-B was essentially unchanged (M3 0.7256/0.7127); H-C raised M3 to 0.7616/0.7357 but removed 22 % of the area, 43 % of detections and 32.5 % of positive cell-days. These results therefore indicate limited, conditional transport, not a successful cross-country replication or a demonstration that M3 is superior to M2.

Two limitations bound the run. First, 19 of 44 M3 features exceed PSI > 0.2 or KS > 0.1 between Formosa and Paraguay-Chaco; the largest shifts are pasture fraction (PSI 1.18), pasture-burning pressure (1.03), forest–agriculture edge (0.51), ecotone index (0.47), minimum temperature (0.25) and 25-km historical density (0.24). Formosa has almost no pasture (median 0 %), whereas the Paraguay-Chaco training distribution is pasture-rich. Second, Open-Meteo was quota-limited during the run, so the climate used CDS precipitation and Hargreaves ET0 rather than the Open-Meteo correction used in Paraguay; this source difference is a sensitivity still to be repeated. An aggregate cross-check against MapBiomas Chaco C5 2023 showed a maximum class-share difference of 5.2 pp (class 6: +4.7 pp), but a pixel-level kappa was not possible because C5 is only available as a Google Earth Engine asset in this environment. A 60-point visual pilot agreed in 53/60 cases (88.3 %); the full 300-point audit remains pending. These results should therefore be read as an exploratory stress test, not as a certified external validation.

| pooled | M2 | 0.7094 | 0.1788 | 0.2145 | 0.1448 | 0.1957 | 0.1869 |
| 2024 | M3 | 0.7245 | 0.1943 | 0.2347 | 0.1385 | 0.2061 | 0.2046 |
| 2025 | M3 | 0.7112 | 0.1716 | 0.2016 | 0.0806 | 0.1551 | 0.2046 |
| pooled | M3 | 0.7184 | 0.1836 | 0.2228 | 0.1123 | 0.1862 | 0.2046 |
| 2024 | FWI | 0.4654 | 0.0841 | 0.0910 | 0.9495 | 0.1111 | 4.0846 |
| 2025 | FWI | 0.4919 | 0.0860 | 0.0918 | 0.8866 | 0.1118 | 4.0846 |
| pooled | FWI | 0.4778 | 0.0849 | 0.0914 | 0.9210 | 0.1114 | 4.0846 |
| 2024 | INPE | 0.4670 | 0.0843 | 0.0883 | 0.8469 | 0.1076 | 0.0486 |
| 2025 | INPE | 0.4658 | 0.0854 | 0.0891 | 0.7845 | 0.1083 | 0.0486 |
| pooled | INPE | 0.4669 | 0.0849 | 0.0886 | 0.8186 | 0.1079 | 0.0486 |

Classic indices were far weaker than either learned model. FWI reached ROC-AUC 0.465 in 2024 and 0.492 in 2025; INPE reached 0.467 and 0.466. Their PR-AUC was 0.084–0.086, below the 0.17–0.19 of M2/M3, and their F0.5 was 0.107–0.112 versus 0.19–0.21. INPE obtained high recall only by alerting almost everything (precision ≈0.09). Thus M2/M3 clearly outperform the Canadian and Brazilian indices in Formosa, but the learned models still do not reach the 0.75 transport threshold. The classic comparison does not rescue the cross-country claim; it only shows that the trained models remain the best available ranking in this domain (Fig. S10).

# Data availability {.unnumbered}

Processed data, test predictions, trained models and derived tables are archived in the v2.0.1 data release (`Incendios_PY_data_v2.0.1.zip`, 1.18 GB) at [github.com/sanchezmartin093-code/Incendios_PY/releases/tag/v2.0.1](https://github.com/sanchezmartin093-code/Incendios_PY/releases/tag/v2.0.1) under CC BY 4.0 and indexed by the data concept DOI [10.5281/zenodo.23675278](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23675278). The v2.1.0 code and tabular artifacts are in the v2.1.0 GitHub release and in `tablas_maestro.xlsx`. Raw NASA FIRMS, ERA5-Land/CDS, MapBiomas, Hansen GFC and geoBoundaries data are obtained from their original providers under their own terms and are documented with SHA-256 hashes in `fuentes/MANIFIESTO_DATOS_v3.csv`. The archived test targets and probabilities are sufficient to regenerate every table and figure in this supplement without downloading the raw multi-terabyte archive.
